Nobody knows where the market opens Monday. You don't need to. What you DO need is a plan for whatever happens.

Mark the levels on the names you trade. Check the calendar (this week has bank earnings, CPI and options expiration). Decide the most you're willing to lose this week, and write it down before the first trade.

What does your Sunday prep look like? 👇

posts.caption:
Every trade costs money before it makes any.

Spreads, commissions and fees come out on every round trip, win or lose. They feel tiny one trade at a time. They are NOT tiny over a year.

5 trades a day at $5 per round trip = $6,300 a year.
20 trades a day at $10 per round trip = $50,400 a year.

That's before a single losing trade. Your strategy has to beat that number first just to break even.

The math: trades a day x cost per round trip x 252 trading days. Before taxes.

How many trades do you make a day? Be honest 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Spreads and fees are the one loss you're guaranteed. Your edge has to beat them first.

The traders who last aren't the ones who trade the most. They're the ones who can sit through 10 "almost" setups and only pull the trigger on the one that actually fits the plan.

Cash is a position too.

posts.caption:
Calls on Friday. Puts on Saturday. Today: the COVERED CALL. Save this. 📌

You own 100 shares at $100 and sell the $105 call for $2.00. You collect $200 today, no matter what happens next.

At expiration:
→ Stock falls to $90: you lose $800 instead of $1,000 (the premium cushions it)
→ Stock stays at $100: you keep the $200
→ Stock at $105 or higher: you make $700, and that's the max. Your shares can get called away at $105

The trade-off is simple: you get paid now, you give up the big upside, and you still own the downside.

What do you want next: cash-secured puts or spreads? 👇

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: A covered call doesn't remove the stock's downside. It only cushions it by the premium.

posts.caption:
Holding a short-dated option and "hoping" is how time decay wins. 🫠

Every day you wait, the option loses a little value. And it's not a straight line: the last few days melt the FASTEST.

That's why so many options go from "down a little" to "worth nothing" in the final week.

Simple fix: decide your exit BEFORE you enter. A profit target, a stop, and a date you'll get out by no matter what.

Ever watched one melt to zero? 👇
posts.comment: Hope is not an exit strategy. Especially with options.

posts.caption:
Would you rather... A or B? 👇

A: Catch the exact bottom once a year, but trade with no rules the rest of the time.
B: Never lose more than 1% on any trade, but never catch a bottom.

Most traders dream about A. It makes the best screenshot.

But the traders still around 10 years later usually live by B. One perfect trade can't fix a hundred careless ones, and a 1% max loss means no single trade can ever knock you out.

A or B? Tell me WHY.
posts.comment: Bottoms make great screenshots. Risk rules make careers.

A missed trade costs $0. A chased trade can cost a lot.

The market makes new setups every single day. You don't need the one that already left.

posts.caption:
Position size is the one decision you control on EVERY trade.

The 1% rule: if your stop gets hit, you lose 1% of your account. Nothing more.

The math: shares = (account x 1%) / (entry price - stop price).

$25,000 account, stop $2 below your entry: 125 shares max.
Same account, stop $5 below: 50 shares.
$10,000 account, $1 stop: 100 shares.

Notice the stop decides the size, not your confidence. A wider stop means fewer shares.

One warning: a stock can gap past your stop overnight, so the real loss can be bigger.

What % do you risk per trade? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:
That gap is the bid-ask spread, and you pay it every time you trade.

Buy at the $1.10 ask, and if you had to sell right away, you'd only get the $0.90 bid. That's an 18% loss before the stock even moves.

Wide spreads usually show up in options with low volume and low open interest.

How to protect yourself:
→ Check volume and open interest before you trade
→ Use limit orders, not market orders
→ Start near the middle of the spread instead of paying the ask

Do you check the spread before you buy? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: A tight spread is a free edge. A wide one is a hidden fee.

The lesson isn't "never trade." It's that every trade needs a real reason, because every trade has a real cost.

Do you overtrade? Be honest 👇

posts.caption:
Implied volatility isn't just a number on your options chain. It's the market's estimate of how far a stock could move.

The math: expected move = price x IV x square root of (days / 365). That's a one standard deviation move, which the stock stays inside about 68% of the time.

On a $100 stock:
→ 20% IV: about ±$1.05 a day, ±$5.73 a month
→ 40% IV: about ±$2.09 a day, ±$11.47 a month
→ 80% IV: about ±$4.19 a day, ±$22.94 a month

Why it matters: if you buy an option, the stock usually has to move MORE than the market already expects for you to win. High IV means you're paying for a big move up front.

Do you check IV before you buy? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

A stop is a decision you made when you were calm. Moving it is a decision you're making when you're scared. Trust the calm version of you.

Before you chase a move this morning, check one thing: is volume higher than normal? If not, be careful.

posts.caption:
Calls, puts, covered calls... today: the CASH-SECURED PUT. Save this. 📌

The stock is at $100. You sell 1 put with a $95 strike for $2.00 and collect $200 today. You set aside $9,500 in cash in case you have to buy 100 shares at $95.

At expiration:
→ Stock stays above $95: the put expires and you keep the $200
→ Stock falls below $95: you buy 100 shares at $95, but your real cost is $93 because of the premium
→ Stock drops to $85: you're down $800 on paper

It's a way to get paid while you wait to buy a stock you already want. The catch: if the stock drops hard, you still own it all the way down.

Only sell puts on stocks you'd be happy to own. Next in the series: spreads?

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:

The first time you move a stop, nothing bad happens. The stock comes back. You feel smart.

So you do it again. And the market eventually finds the one time it doesn't come back.

Rule worth tattooing on your monitor: stops only move in ONE direction, toward locking in profit. Never further away from your entry.

posts.caption:

The catch with A: it's a job. Some months it pays more. Some months it pays nothing, or less than nothing.

One buys your time back. The other trades your time for money. A or B, and why?

Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:

A loss that teaches you something is part of the process. A loss you repeat three times is just a habit you haven't faced yet.

After every losing trade, write down three things: what happened, what you felt, and which rule you broke (if any). It takes two minutes.

Read it back once a week. The pattern will jump out at you.

posts.caption:
This is the part of selling options nobody explains until it happens to you.

Most stock options in the U.S. are American-style: the buyer can exercise any time before expiration. If you sold that option, you can be ASSIGNED early.

Sold a covered call? Your shares can get called away. Sold a put? You can be handed 100 shares per contract.
Early assignment is most likely when an option is deep in the money, or right before a dividend for calls.

Index options like SPX are different: they're European-style and cash-settled, so no early assignment.

Trading desks give every trader a daily loss limit. Most people trading from home never set one.

Why it matters: three bad days in a row costs you 6%. Annoying, but fixable. One day of revenge trading can cost 20%, and a 20% loss needs a +25% gain just to get back to even.

posts.caption:
Delta tells you more than how fast an option moves. It's also a rough probability.

Rule of thumb: an option's delta is about its chance of finishing in the money. Its chance of TOUCHING the strike before expiration is about double that.

Example: you sell a 0.20 delta put.
→ About a 20% chance it finishes in the money
→ About a 40% chance the stock trades through your strike at some point before expiration

That's why option sellers get tested far more often than they expect. Your strike getting hit is not rare. Plan for it before you sell.

These are model approximations, not guarantees. Big news can blow right through them.

Do you check delta before you pick a strike? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

Calls, puts, covered calls, cash-secured puts... today: the BULL CALL SPREAD. Save this. 📌

The stock is at $100. You buy the $100 call for $4.00 and sell the $110 call for $1.50. Your net cost is $250, and that's the most you can lose.

At expiration:
→ Below $100: you lose the $250
→ At $102.50: break-even
→ At $110 or higher: you make the max, $750

The trade-off: you give up everything above $110 to cut your cost from $400 to $250. A smaller bet with a clear max loss and a clear max win.

This is the options mistake that costs money without anyone noticing.

Example: the stock is at $110. Your $100 call trades at $12.00 with weeks left.

→ Exercise: you buy the stock at $100 when it's worth $110. That's $1,000 of value per contract.
→ Sell the call: you collect $1,200.

The $200 difference is time value, and exercising early throws it away.

Exceptions exist, like deep in-the-money calls right before a dividend, or contracts with very wide bid-ask spreads. Most of the time, selling to close wins.

My wife and I have a 20-minute money talk every Sunday night. It's the most boring part of our week. It's also saved us a LOT of arguments.

We don't do spreadsheets from hell. We go through 4 things:
→ What came in this week
→ What went out (and anything that surprised us)
→ What's coming up (birthdays, car stuff, school things)
→ One thing we're working toward

That's it. No judgment, no "why did you buy that." Just information.

Here's what I've noticed: most money fights aren't really about money. They're about surprises. When you both know what's going on, there's nothing to fight about.

The stock market moves every single day, but most of those moves are noise. A stock can be down 2% on Tuesday for no reason anyone will remember next year. When you check constantly, you see every one of those wiggles, and your brain treats each one like news you have to act on.

That's where the damage happens:
→ Red days trigger fear, and fear says "sell before it gets worse"
→ Green days trigger greed, and greed says "buy more of whatever's hot"
→ Both push you to trade more, and trading more usually means paying more and earning less

Behavioral researchers have a name for part of this: loss aversion. A loss tends to feel about twice as painful as a same-sized gain feels good. So the more often you look, the more often you feel that pain, and the more likely you are to do something you regret.

What actually builds wealth is boring:
→ Invest automatically on a set schedule
→ Keep fees low
→ Decide your plan once, then leave it alone
→ Check on purpose (once a month is plenty), not out of anxiety

→ Someone earning $150,000 who leases a new car, lives in the biggest place they qualify for, and has almost nothing invested
→ Someone earning $55,000 who drives an old car, invests 15% of every paycheck, and quietly builds a fortune

Here's the math on that second person. 15% of $55,000 is $8,250 a year. Invested every year for 25 years at a 7% average return, that grows to about $521,805. On a "normal" salary.

The difference was never the income. It's the gap between what comes in and what goes out, and what happens to that gap.

How to turn a salary into wealth:
→ Know your savings rate (what % of take-home pay you keep)
→ Pay yourself first: invest on payday, before you spend
→ Raise your savings rate every time your income goes up
→ Put the gap into long-term investments, not a checking account

A big salary with a big lifestyle is a treadmill. A normal salary with a steady gap, invested for years, is how most real wealth gets built.

10 investing mistakes that cost Americans the most, counted down. Number one is the one almost everybody makes. 👇

10. Thinking you need a lot to start. Many big brokers sell fractional shares for as little as $1 to $5.

posts.caption:
Roth IRA: pay tax on the seed, not the tree. 🌱🌳

If I could explain one investing account to every 22-year-old, it would be this one.

Here's how a Roth IRA works, in plain English:
→ You put in money you've already paid income tax on (the seed)
→ You invest it, often in simple index funds
→ It can grow for decades, and you don't pay tax on that growth
→ In retirement, qualified withdrawals come out tax-free (the tree)

So you pay tax on a small seed today instead of on a big tree later.

The 2026 numbers: you can put in up to $7,500 a year, or $8,600 if you're 50 or older.

The fine print, honestly:
→ There are income limits on who can contribute directly
→ "Qualified" generally means you're 59½ or older and the account is at least 5 years old
→ You can usually take out what you contributed (not the growth) at any time

Why it's so powerful for younger investors: the earlier you plant the seed, the bigger the tree gets, and none of that growth is taxed if you follow the rules.

posts.caption:
Losses hurt twice as much as gains feel good. 😣

This isn't just a feeling. It's one of the most famous findings in behavioral economics. Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky found that a loss tends to hit us roughly twice as hard as an equal gain feels good. They called it loss aversion.

It sounds harmless, but it quietly wrecks a lot of portfolios:
→ We sell winners too early to "lock in" the good feeling
→ We hold losers way too long because selling makes the loss feel real
→ We check our accounts constantly, and every red day stings more than the green days help
→ We avoid investing at all, because a possible loss feels worse than the cost of doing nothing

That last one is sneaky. Cash on the sidelines feels safe, but over time inflation slowly eats it.

How to work with your brain instead of against it:
→ Decide your exit rules before you buy, while you're calm
→ Look at your portfolio less often, so you see fewer painful dips
→ Judge decisions by your process, not by one result
→ For long-term money, automate it so your emotions don't get a vote

You can't turn off loss aversion. But once you know it's there, you can stop letting it trade for you.

Every stock market crash felt like the end of the world. Here's how long the comeback actually took. 👇

→ Black Monday, 1987: the S&P 500 fell 20.5% in ONE day. It was back above its old high by July 1989, under two years later.
→ The dot-com bust, 2000: the S&P 500 fell about 49% and needed seven years to get back (March 2000 to May 2007). The tech-heavy Nasdaq took about fifteen.

→ Covid, 2020: down about 34% in just over a month, then a new record close on August 18, 2020.
→ 2022: down about 25%, then a new record on January 19, 2024, roughly two years after the old high.

Two lessons hide in that list. Recoveries are real, but they aren't always fast, and the ones that took longest started with sky-high prices. That's why money you need soon doesn't belong in stocks, and why owning the whole market beats betting on the hottest corner of it.

The people who got hurt most usually weren't the ones who held. They were the ones who sold near the bottom and waited for it to "feel safe" again.

Time in the market beats timing the market. ⏱️

Trying to time the market means getting two decisions right: when to get out AND when to get back in. Miss either one and you can do worse than if you'd just stayed put.

The tricky part is that the market's best days tend to show up right next to its worst ones. J.P. Morgan found that 7 of the S&P 500's 10 best days over a recent 20-year period came within two weeks of the 10 worst days. So if you sell in a panic, there's a real chance you miss the rebound too.

What staying invested looks like in practice:
→ Invest on a schedule, not on a feeling
→ Expect drops, they're part of the deal
→ Don't sell long-term money because of short-term news
→ Give your plan years to work, not weeks

I don't know where the market goes next week. Nobody does. I just know I want to be in it when the good days show up.

My entire investing strategy fits in one sentence: same amount, same day, every month. 📅

It's called dollar-cost averaging, and the logic is simple:
→ When prices are high, my money buys fewer shares
→ When prices fall, the same money buys MORE shares
→ Over time, I never have to guess the "right" moment

The real benefit isn't math, it's psychology. When the plan is automatic, there's no decision to agonize over when the market is scary, and no temptation to go all-in when it's euphoric.

A few honest notes:
→ It doesn't guarantee a profit or protect against losses
→ If you already have a big lump sum, the research often favors investing it sooner rather than later
→ For most people investing from each paycheck, it's simply the natural way to invest

The hardest month to keep buying is the one where everything is red. That's usually the month the plan helps the most.

Do you invest on a schedule or when it "feels right"? 👇

posts.caption:
Why selling a loser is so much harder than it should be. 🧠

When a stock is down, selling makes the loss "real." Holding lets us pretend it might still work out. Behavioral economists call this the disposition effect: people tend to sell winners too early and hold losers too long.

It comes from loss aversion. A loss hurts roughly twice as much as an equal gain feels good (Kahneman & Tversky), so we'll do almost anything to avoid locking one in, including watching it get worse.

The question that helped me: "If I had this money in cash today, would I buy this stock at this price?"
→ If yes, hold it, and you have a real reason
→ If no, you're only holding it to avoid feeling wrong

Other things that help:
→ Decide your exit plan before you buy
→ Judge decisions by your process, not one outcome
→ Remember that every good investor is wrong regularly. Staying wrong is the expensive part

Being wrong is part of investing. Refusing to admit it is optional.

Ever held a loser way too long? 👇

-Cole

(Loss aversion: Kahneman & Tversky, prospect theory.)

The best time to make a crash plan is when there's no crash. 📝

When the market drops 20% or 30%, your brain isn't at its best. Headlines are loud, your account is red, and every instinct says "do something." That's exactly when people make the decisions they regret most.

So I made the decision ahead of time and wrote it down. My crash plan is three lines:
→ Keep investing my normal amount on schedule
→ Check my account no more than once a month
→ Don't sell long-term investments because of short-term news

A few things that make a plan like this realistic:
→ Have an emergency fund, so you're never forced to sell low to pay bills
→ Only invest money you won't need for at least five years
→ Know that big drops are normal. From 1980 to 2023, the S&P 500 had an average drop of about 14% at some point during the year and still finished positive in 33 of 44 years (J.P. Morgan)

Your plan doesn't have to look like mine. It just has to exist before you need it.

What's in your crash plan? 👇

-Cole

The cheapest edge in trading: writing things down. 📓

Most traders remember their wins and forget their losses. A trading journal fixes that, because you can't argue with your own handwriting.

What to write for every trade:
→ Entry price and why you got in
→ Your plan: where you'll get out if you're wrong, and if you're right
→ Position size
→ How you felt when you placed it (bored, excited, revenge, FOMO)
→ What actually happened, and whether you followed the plan

After a few weeks, patterns jump off the page. For a lot of people, the losing trades cluster around the same emotions: trading out of boredom, chasing after a big green candle, or trying to win back a loss.

Once you can see the pattern, you can build a rule against it.

The goal isn't to never lose. It's to stop losing the same way twice.

What to do right after a big trading loss: probably nothing. 🚶

A big loss sets off a chain reaction in your head: frustration, then urgency, then the need to "make it back" right now. That's how one bad trade turns into three.

Why stepping away works:
→ Your judgment is weakest right after a loss
→ The urge to win it back pushes you into bigger, worse trades
→ Nothing about the market requires you to act in the next hour

Rules a lot of disciplined traders use:
→ A daily loss limit. Hit it and you're done for the day
→ A mandatory break after a losing trade
→ No increasing position size to recover losses
→ Review the trade in your journal before placing the next one

The market opens again tomorrow. Make sure your account is still in good enough shape to show up.

Why compounding feels like nothing is happening, until it really is. 📈

Here's $500 a month invested at a 7% average return:
→ After 10 years: about $86,542 (you put in $60,000)
→ After 20 years: about $260,463 (you put in $120,000)
→ After 30 years: about $609,985 (you put in $180,000)

In the first decade, most of the balance is just your own money. It feels slow, almost pointless. By year 30, most of it is growth, and the last 10 years add more than the first 20 combined.

That's why people quit early: the boring part is front-loaded and the exciting part comes last.

How to survive the boring decade:
→ Automate your contributions so they don't depend on motivation
→ Stop checking your balance every week
→ Measure progress by consistency, not by the number
→ Raise your contribution whenever your income grows

If it feels boring, it's probably working.

Nobody can predict the market. So build a plan that doesn't need you to. 🧭

Most investing mistakes come from plans that only work if you're right: going all in on one stock, timing the market, using money you'll need soon. When you're wrong, and everyone is sometimes, those plans break.

A plan that survives being wrong usually has:
→ Diversification, so no single bet can sink you
→ A long time horizon, so short-term drops don't force you to sell
→ An emergency fund, so you never have to sell at a bad time
→ Position sizing, so one bad trade can't wipe you out
→ Automatic contributions, so emotions don't get a vote

None of these make you right more often. They make being wrong a lot less expensive.

The investors who last aren't the ones with the best predictions. They're the ones whose plans can take a hit and keep going.
